preamble: Loss of pharyngealization in the emphatic interdental [ðˤ], Arabic ẓāʾ ظ, which becomes plain [ð]. The documented case is loan adaptation in Swahili. Most of its Arabic loanwords come from Omani Arabic (Wikipedia, Swahili), and they render ظ with dh, the voiced dental fricative /ð/, which Wikipedia's Swahili consonant table lists in parentheses: ظَنّ ẓann > dhana, ظُلْم ẓulm > dhuluma. Wikipedia, citing Lodhi (2003), adds that in some Arabic loans speakers reproduce the original emphatics /dˤ sˤ tˤ ðˤ/ to express emphasis or intensity. Loans from ḍād ض are not counted here, because the sources consulted do not give the value of ḍ in the donor speech. In Classical Arabic ẓāʾ was a velarized [ðˠ] and in Modern Standard Arabic it is a pharyngealized [ðˤ] (Wikipedia, Ẓāʾ). Persian, Urdu and Turkish instead borrowed ẓāʾ as plain [z] (Versteegh 1999, cited by Wikipedia), a different outcome.

examples.from: Arabic ظَنّ ẓann, verbal noun of ظَنَّ 'to think, suppose'
examples.note: The verb ظَنَّ gives Swahili dhani (Wiktionary, Descendants).

examples.from: Arabic ظَالِم ẓālim, active participle of ظَلَمَ 'to wrong, oppress'
examples.to: Swahili dhalimu 'unjust person, tyrant; cruel, unjust'

examples.note: Word-final ẓ, with an epenthetic vowel before it and a final -i.
